scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): agrees with the claim and largely with its reason while arguing for flexibility; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Truly educated people are often thought to know something about many fields, not just one.
One claim holds that universities should require students to take courses outside their major, on the reason that knowing various disciplines is the best way to become truly educated.
I agree with the claim and largely with its reason, though I believe the requirement should leave some room for choice.

sections.role: Body 1 — Agreeing with the claim and reason

sentences.text: First, the reason behind the claim is largely sound, because broad knowledge does make people more truly educated.
Studying many disciplines lets students see how different fields connect and inform one another.
For example, a literature student who also learns some science can think about the world more completely.
This shows that a varied education produces a richer and more flexible mind.
Knowing several disciplines also helps people understand complex problems that cross many fields at once.
Such breadth builds the kind of judgment that a narrow training alone can never provide.
To this extent, the claim and its reason clearly deserve support.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why the requirement needs flexibility

sentences.text: Second, however, the requirement should be applied flexibly rather than forced on everyone in the same way.
Students already carry heavy workloads, and too many required courses can crowd out their main subject.
Consider a medical student whose demanding schedule leaves very little time for many extra classes.
Forcing wide breadth in such cases could weaken the deep training her career truly requires.
A wiser policy lets students choose their outside courses from a broad range rather than dictating each one.
Breadth and depth, after all, are both necessary parts of a complete education.
The reason holds best, then, when breadth is encouraged without crushing depth.
In conclusion, requiring some study outside the major does help students become truly educated.
But the requirement should stay flexible enough to protect the depth each field demands.
The best universities give students wide horizons while still guarding the focus of their main study.
